PRESENTATION OF SEVENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the seventh report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which deals with the agri-food program of the Department of Agriculture. The committee is concerned that farm income programs need to be more carefully planned, funded and co-ordinated to ensure that adequate reserves are built up to assist farmers at times of greatest need. This is highlighted by the recent dramatic increase in the western grain stabilization fund deficit which has risen to $850 million in April, 1987, from $175 million on December 31, 1986. A need for better information and analysis in the administration of this program is required, as well as better information to the Minister in the exercise of discretionary authority.
Your committee is concerned also about the health hazard posed by inadequate procedures and facilities for the storage and disposal of dangerous substances. This problem had been noted in earlier reports and therefore your committee will pay particular attention to the Department's aim of 100 per cent compliance for the handling, transporting, storing and disposing of these materials.
As a result of two cases in London, Ontario, involving major capital projects which demonstrated a lack of consciousness, the committee is calling on the Department to demonstrate its capacity to accept increased responsibility and to be cost conscious in the expenditure of taxpayers' money.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INQUIRY INTO USE OF CHEMICAL PESTICIDES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106. The petitioners reside in Hinton, Grande Cache, Rimbey, Lethbridge, Red Deer, Condor, Edmonton, Camrose, Calgary, Jasper, Drayton Valley, Robb, Sherwood Park, St. Albert, Stony Plain, Edson, and other locations in Alberta. The petitioners are of the opinion that increasing numbers of chemicals used as herbicides and insecticides are being proven to have harmful effects on human health. They believe these chemicals also produce short and long-term harmful effects on non-target organisms, soil and water, and that the same chemicals in past years have been registered and approved as safe for their various uses. The petitioners therefore call upon the House of Commons to initiate a full public inquiry into the safety, testing, registration and regulation of the use of pesticides and an examination of alternative ways of controlling pests such as biological control and plant-derived pesticides.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Claudy Mailly (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is incredible that, today, the Government should have to defend an institution as prestigious as the National Film Board. However, because of a motion by the New Democratic Party to substract $100,000 from the National Film Board's budget, the Government of Canada has a duty to defend an institution that has made its mark in the cultural and social sphere in this country.
The reputation of the NFB has been recognized by the public, and in fact internationally, for many years. And each year's production confirms that this reputation is not exaggerated, witness the NFB's latest productions under the directorship of Fran?ois Macerola and his team. We have every reason to be proud of an institution that is one of the great success stories in Canada's cultural history.
Since it obtained its initial mandate, the NFB has been producing and distributing films, and now videos, and plays a major and strategic role in the world of the motion picture industry, culture and communications, where public and private institutions work side by side. In this respect, the NFB is an essential adjunct to our country.
It helps provide Canadians with basically Canadian cultural products that respond to their expectations and their needs, Madam Speaker, and which offer a comprehensive view of our own reality and culture.
The NFB's primary role is to help Canadians become aware of their own cultural identity, to enhance their knowledge of what they are and of the values by which our society is defined. Because of its mandate, the NFB is not subject to the same financial constraints as the private sector. It is therefore our responsibility, here in the House, Madam Speaker, to ensure it has the means to carry out that mandate.
That does not mean the National Film Board, as a State-funded filmmaking agency, can afford to neglect current developments in the industry. Several years ago, it established a number of objectives for institutional renewal which have helped to make its organization less unwieldy and more flexible, and as a result, the NFB has been able to introduce more efficient operations and filmmaking practices. Building on the experience acquired over the years, the NFB has
Supply
rejuvenated its image and while stimulating the creativity of in-house filmmakers it has also attracted independent film artists who increasingly are taking advantage of the institution's new open policy in this respect.
This publicly-funded producer is becoming increasingly better equipped to fulfil a mandate that is particularly important today. Its success and its image are due first of all to the daring, quality and excellence of NFB productions which respond to the social and cultural needs of Canadians. Fiction feature films, documentaries and thematic subjects all reflect a Canadian reality. In addition, the NFB also plays a role in developing and advancing filmmaking techniques.
One example is the development of the IMAX Three-D, which was used to make the first production to be actually projected in 3D. Madam Speaker, I am referring to the film Canadians had the pleasure of seeing at Expo 86 in Vancouver. This film was seen by about 700,000 visitors from all over North America and the rest of the world.
Madam Speaker, I would also like to mention a fond memory. During Expo '67 in Montreal, the city where I was born, the NFB presented a film which people are still talking about. It was screened in the Fabyrinth Pavilion where film producer Roman Kroiter and his assistant Joan Henson, a close friend of mine with whom I attended McGill University, had prepared an absolutely extraordinary documentary highlighting Canada's cinematographic evolution. It was the NFB which provided these highly talented young Canadians with an opportunity to produce this film at the pavilion, a film which earned general plaudits at Expo '67. As early as 1967 therefore, 20 years ago, the NFB made a name for itself and for Canada in the realm of cinematography.
The NFB continues to be very active on a number of research and development fronts, experimenting with new techniques and thus keeping abreast of state-of-the-art technologies which it uses to its own ends and from which cinematographic circles in Canada and abroad can readily benefit.
A visit to National Film Board headquarters is all one needs to see how very succesful it has been. The walls are literally covered with plaques and awards attesting to the excellence of its productions.
One hundred and forty-six NFB productions were singled out for awards during the last fiscal year: 69 here in Canada, 40 in the United States, 39 in Europe, and one in Australia. The Decline of the American Empire alone accounts for 18 awards.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I would draw Hon. Members' attention to a special program designed to warn children against sexual abuses. This has to be the current topic with which we can all readily identify, and here again the NFB is leading the way. I am referring to the series Mon corps, c'est mon corps which is distributed by public organizations throughout Canada. In recent months this series has sold 7,686


Supply
video copies and the NFB is planning to send 3,500 videocassettes to public libraries from coast to coast.
Such success can only stem from the NFB growing popularity and the need for this kind of agency. Fully aware of current trends, the NFB has revamped its distribution network to make its products more readily accessible. Ever more organizations are promoting and distributing NFB films because its products are increasingly geared to a variety of needs. The number of Canadian viewers is on the increase and sales abroad are booming.
The National Film Board is responsible also for training our filmmarkers and upgrading their skills. Together with departments and provincial agencies, the NFB has developed experimental training programs dealing with various moviemaking trades, as a result of which we are witnessing a new breed of people increasingly skilled in their craft, to meet the needs of our own producers and those of foreign producers who come to make movies in Canada.
Moreover, the NFB is making every effort to attract a larger audience by ensuring its presence on the national television networks during prime time, as well as on the educational networks. Over the past two years, the English and French national networks added more and more NFB productions to their programming.
Moreover, the NFB has been trying, in its programming to reach the various strata of our Canadian society, supplying with quality videos institutions such as video clubs, film archives and film theatres, as well as video distributing machines. Also in the area of broadcasting, the Government Film Commissioner tabled recently with the CRTC a request for licenses to be issued to Tele-Canada and TV-Canada, which will specialize in public interest non-commercial television services.
In line with the Caplan-Sauvageau Report recommendations, these services would serve essentially to identify Canadian social and cultural realities, to represent Canada in its entirety, to broadcast quality programs, to give Canadians, both men and women, with creative abilities better access to television, and to provide complementary programs.
That kind of project evidently reflects the will of the NFB to have the widest distribution possible for its productions. This is a necessity as important as the capacity to produce, Madam Speaker. Why have excellent films if people cannot see them? So this is a necessity for which funds are required. This is not the time to reduce the funds; we should rather try to add to the existing funds. This is why, breaking new grounds in the distribution area, the NFB has concluded agreements with public and school libraries to make them partners in the distribution of its films and videos.
That kind of agreement is very successful. I will give only one example but it is without doubt very telling. In 1984-85, the city of Quebec public library rented 335 videocassettes and 254 were viewed on the premises. However, following the signature of the agreement, in 1985-86, that is under our
government, Madam Speaker, the renting of videocassettes went up to 5,525 and then to 8,070 in the first nine months of the following financial year; to that number must be added 3,700 internal viewings. Therefore, we realize, Madam Speaker how much public access to viewing has increased.
The countless successes of the National Film Board are not due to chance. They are due in the first place to experienced personnel which can be found at every level of the organization. They are due also to the leadership of the Commissioner and his management team. The NFB was not afraid to set itself some high objectives and does not hesitate to innovate and encourage creativity. As a public producer, the NFB provides support to all talented filmmakers everywhere in Canada. In fact, 70 per cent of NFB films are made by freelance filmmakers, a major contribution to the development of new talents and the growth of our cinematographic industry.
Madam Speaker, another plus is the very special consideration given women by the NFB which has set up mechanisms to promote the cultural constituency they so properly deserve. Whatever one may say, Madam Speaker, whatever the NDP opposition may claim, the Access and Equality program is aimed at wage parity and employment equity for women working at the NFB. Under this program launched last year, it is expected that parity between male and female permanent and casual NFB staff will have been achieved by 1996.
In this respect, Madam Speaker, it must be recalled that in 1974 the NFB created a separate unit-Studio D-to meet the specific needs of women film producers and English-speaking viewers. This is the special domain of anglophone women filmmakers. Through this unit the NFB makes it possible for women to produce films and provides them with an opportunity to become proficient in every sectors of cinematography. Ever since it opened its doors, Studio D has gained international recognition for the quality of its productions.
So those are some of the accomplishments which were made under the aegis of Franqois Macerola and which ought to be kept in mind. We must be fully aware of them and realize how enriching they are for all Canadians, men and women alike. Are we going to take a stingy axe to such a cultural heritage? Are we going to deprive our filmmakers-even partially-of such an essential tool for our own development?
The NFB is a large and diversified public undertaking. It has already agreed to make major budget cut-backs, thus contributing to reduce the national deficit, as would any agency or ministry of a Government intent on setting public finances back on an even keel. Even at that the NFB has managed to fund its activities and come up with new programs. At the present time, the socio-cultural balance of Canada's cinematographic industry rests squarely on three production sectors: film production by women, regional production, and production of fiction feature films. These three creation sectors deserve the financial backing required for more dynamic expansion.


We owe the NFB the support it needs to carry on with its activities. It would be an unfathomable loss, Madam Speaker, for the private and public movie industry if our public producer were to be forced to reduce its involvement in areas of activities that are so important to each and everyone of us.
In this vast country of ours, with a number of remote isolated communities, movies play an essential role as an outstanding communication medium. We should give the film industry all our support and even increase that effort so that it can serve the Canadian people even better, rather than calling for cuts in its funding.
The suggestion under consideration bears the mark of ignorance, or at least of inexplicable blindness, and is therefore unacceptable. Such a lack of common sense is beyond belief, Madam Speaker. The motion calls for cuts of $100,000 out of a $72 million budget, for reasons which appear to be rather personal. I read the report of an exchange which took place at the Standing committee between the Hon. Member in whose name this motion for $100,000 cut stands and Mr. Macerola, and I must say that I was taken aback by the personal and agressive remarks of that person, and that I felt very sad when I read that text, because I deeply respect the Hon. Member who moved that resolution. I am surprised at the approach she has decided to embark upon for reasons which she will no doubt be explaining to us later on.
Deep in the memory and in the experience of every Canadian man and woman, there is a character, a lansdcape, a situation, which have helped them know and understand themselves better. We could all mention a movie of the NFB, a documentary which made us feel proud to be Canadians.
Let us think for instance of the innovation of Mr. MacLar-en. 1 remember as a child, as a teenager at school, when we were shown those outstanding short films.
Just skimming through the 300 pages of the NFB inventory will provide an answer for everyone. The NFB is our collective memory, and that past and present memory deserves to be respected and protected. Presently, the National Film Board needs us and is asking us to let it keep its share of the development of the Canadian movie industry.
As we are the ones who need the NFB, Madam Speaker, we will agree with that request out of generosity and self-respect, and we will reject in no uncertain terms the suggestion of the New Democratic opposition.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it may seem to be quite an anomaly, and indeed it is, for me to be proposing a cut of $100,000 from the budget of the National Film Board because I am a long-term supporter of the National Film Board. I have protested against the very substantial cuts the Government ordered against the NFB and which have been defended by the Parliamentary Secretary who is going to the rescue. She is trying to defend against my proposal today, which is for a very specific purpose, and I will explain very precisely why. This is a symbolic gesture. The $100,000 that I propose be cut from the budget of the NFB represents the salary and benefits to the President of the NFB who has acted in a most irresponsible way. I intend to document to this House precisely in what kind of irresponsible fashion he has acted and why he is unworthy to be the head of the NFB.
I would like to see the NFB get lots more money, not just $100,000 more. I think it could use far more money than that.
1 have supported it in principle being involved a TV Tele-Canada proposal, which not everyone does, but I want to see the NFB involved in that.
I have opposed the drastic cuts suggested for the NFB in the past by government commissions, task forces and so forth. So I am a supporter and I am very disappointed about the way it is acting on the very important question of funding films for women, its own Studio D in English production and, of course, it is not making a priority for women in French production.
Studio D has been very important for women in this country. It has been a means of expression for women. It has given an opportunity for women film makers who, after all, have a much tougher time getting independent film money. The role of funding film makers who are women is absolutely essential for women to have voice and to be part of the world of film and video in Canada.
There has been a long history of attacks on Studio D. I can recall when I was President of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women defending Studio D when it was always about to be cut completely. We had to run to its defence because it was speaking for women in a way in which no other body was. I note also that the model of Studio D has been proposed as a model to emulate in other institutions. The Caplan-Sauvageau report, for example, made a recommendation that Studio D, the women's arm of the NFB, should be seen as an important player in the NFB's contribution to TV Canada, its expertise in producing women's films serving as a model to the entire broadcasting industry. I very much agree with this assessment. I think it is quite right.
I recall that for women trying to get the CBC to have more women producers, directors and more broadcasting reflecting women's points of view in an area where women were still


Supply
badly represented, Studio D was a positive model and it is a very important part of our cultural life.
I have been raising this issue with the President of the NFB when he comes before the committee for Estimates. I want to quote what was actually said. He came before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in 1985 on Estimates. I asked him about the role for Studio D. Mr. Macerola turned the responsibility of answering my question over to Mrs. Joan Pennefather, the Vice-Commissioner and Planning Director. She said: "The NFB is stating quite clearly its continuing support for women's production at the NFB and in Canada". With respect to production both in Studio D and by Francophone women at the Film Board she said: "We are not only supporting the continuance of Studio D but the expansion of its mandate, a national mandate to reach out to Anglophone and Francophone women". She goes on to say: "There it is, its work is continuing. It is not satisfactory and we want it to grow". She also talked about expansion.
1 have already pressed them on the need to have an equivalent studio for Francophone women since Studio D makes only Anglophone productions. There has been a great demand for that. There has been a demand for the great films of Studio D to be subtitled in French so that they will be accessible. That has not been allowed, or at least not in nearly adequate numbers.
1 suggested that in terms of popularity, rentals and sales Studio D is actually Studio A. In terms of winning prizes Studio D is Studio A. Indeed, when I suggested this in committee, the President of the National Film Board, Mr. Macerola, said: "Yes, you are absolutely right. Yes". I asked him about funding and why the studio was not getting more.
As to the discussion about the exact amount of money that it was getting, Mr. Macerola said: "The object is to increase that budget". This is from the transcript of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture for May 9, 1985, at page 12:23. That is a very specific promise.
On the next page, page 12:24, Mr. Macerola states:
We are just in the middle of the exercise of allocating the financial resources. It will be the normal increase . . . but that is not enough.
I cannot give you a precise figure. Nevertheless, the objective is to increase the budget of Studio D and to increase the amount of money devoted to film making by women at the NFB. It will be a significant and a very important increase, but I cannot tell you the percentage because we are in the middle of it.
Nevertheless, significant and important suggests significant and important-large, not small. We have been promised a significant increase, and that was before a parliamentary committee which represents not only Parliament but the people of Canada in vetting the estimates of the National Film Board. It is what the President of the National Film Board promised.
What did he do? He did not increase the budget of Studio D. We know that in the meantime the NFB experienced cuts.
But when we look at the period from 1985 until 1987, although there were cuts, that money has been restored. If we look under the heading "English Programming Financial Resource Allocation" for women's production, we see that the actual figure for 1985-86 is $2,531,000. The estimate for 1987-88 is down to $2,184,000. For marketing the figure for 1985-86 was $288,000 and for 1987-88 it is down to $228,000. These are decreases, not increases. Yet we had a promise of significant increases.
The total resources in this area of course have gone up. The total for production in 1985-86 was $22,960,000, whereas by 1987-88 the figure had increased to $24,939,000. For marketing there had been an increase from $4,079,000 to $4,715,000. This is a section of the Film Board that has had an increase in its allocations while Studio D has gone down. It has gone down in proportion, and it has gone down in actual figures. Yet the President promised an increase, and a significant one.
The Parliamentary Secretary thinks that my reaction is a personal one, as if it were somehow a peculiar reaction for a Member of Parliament who sits on the committee. The Parliamentary Secretary did not sit on the committee. She did not hear that promise. But she can look it up in the minutes of the committee meeting and see that he made a promise to the committee of a significant increase. She can read right in front of her that there is a real decrease. That is not a personal reaction. Here we have the President of the National Film Board making a promise to a parliamentary committee and then reneging on it and cutting the money.
If one turns the page in the Estimates to the next page and looks at French productions, one will see that women's productions are not even on the list-so much for making it a priority area for Francophone producers, directors and performers. This is something which has been demanded before.
The National Film Board likes to talk about its employment equity program. I applaud it for introducing an employment equity program. Every government Department and every enterprise of any size ought to have one. I am not against it. I have said before that I am in favour of it. I am pleased to see that it has one. Women should be able to move into other roles. Women should be part of every studio at the National Film Board. They should have opportunities for training and promotion, of course. But that is not a substitute for having Studio D, or a Francophone equivalent of Studio D. Women must feel so at home at the Film Board that they can get their ideas across so that there is not a situation of women film makers having to go to male managers of departments or studios and asking and trying to convince them that their point of view, while it might be a bit different, is nevertheless worthy.
We have to accept the fact that there may be differences of opinion as to what is the best way to do things artistically. There is a difference. Vive la difference. We want to see that the creativity of women and men has a chance to be explored. While there is a managerial structure that is overwhelmingly


male and women have to go to male managers to ask for money, that is not adequate. There may be a time in which Studio D is not needed. That may happen. But I do not see it happening yet. Until that happens we need a strong Studio D.
I can give Hon. Members an example of what the President of the Film Board said himself. This is from the committee hearings held on May 21, 1987. Again, he was being asked about Studio D. Mr. Macerola states, as reported on page 42:22:
-well, I have some problems, frankly speaking, with the filmic approach of
certain films. I think they are putting too much emphasis on the content but
nevertheless,... this film is returning some good revenues.
From Mr. Macerola's perspective he does not like some of the work that Studio D does. He is entitled to his opinion. But it is important that there be a studio where women can make the decisions about what is film quality and not have to answer to a male manager who may have a different opinion. It seems to me only fair that that should be the case. Women should have a chance to explore and to use their creative abilities. If they have some differences, they should be expressed, just as men express theirs. In the meantime-we want to see women moving into positions in other studios and being able to do their work in other studios working with men.
When we have the situation of Mr. Macerola lying to a parliamentary committee, not fulfilling his promises, what do we do? The idea of having a separate vote for Studio D, to have a National Film Board women's division, seems to be not the way we like to do things in Canada. We like to have women and men working together. While we have a situation in which women have been very under-represented, not appointed to managerial positions and not being given any opportunities for expressing themselves, having a separate studio for Anglophone women and a separate studio for Francophone women makes sense. That is a reasonable Canadian type of compromise. The idea of having a completely and separate parliamentary vote, a completely separate board of directors and so forth seems to me to be going too far. That kind of separation of women and men is not what we want. I would like to think that women and men can by and large work together. But while women are still not on an equal basis in reality with men, we need two studios, by language, in which women can have their own voices heard.
I think the idea of having a separate vote and so forth, going to those lengths, is wrong. I am not suggesting we go that route. But I can tell Hon. Members that I feel very much puzzled as to what else we can do. I do not think we can continue with a President of the Film Board who comes to a committee and who admits that the studio is doing good work and who promises it extra money and then reneges on that promise. What is a parliamentary committee for if people will come before it and not do what they actually say they will do? We have to be able to count on the heads of agencies who come before us. If their word is not good, we have to get rid of those people and bring in people who will actually do the jobs properly and will be fair to both women and men.
Supply
If progress is made in employment equity, that is fine. I understand that some new appointments are coming up and I am very pleased to see that. We will certainly applaud any move in that direction. Women have been appointed as head of the camera department, head of the Atlantic regional office and recently head of the Pacific regional office in Vancouver. It is very good to see these appointments and no one is complaining about them. However, until there is real equality between men and women, we must see adequate funding for Studio D.
I note that an advisory committee for Studio D composed of people both in and out of the Film Board, film-makers and representatives of women's organizations across Canada, recommended that Studio D needed $3 million to $5 million to do its job. The people who made this recommendation know the Film Board and its capacity for work. They know what can be done. This year, $2,154,000 has been awarded to Studio D. That is not terribly close to what the advisory committee indicated would be sufficient.
Mr. Macerola has said that 36 per cent of English film production will be done by women this year. That figure does not sound too bad. It is not 50 per cent or 52 per cent, but it is not a bad figure. I note, however, that it is a bit of an exaggeration because the Daughters of the Earth program took a very large amount of money. There is a little blip from that and normally the participation of women is not nearly that good. Yet the quality of the films produced by Studio D is very good. Those films win awards all around the world. They are very popular. Canadian people watch them, rent them and buy them. They are sold in other countries as well.
A study done by Chris Scherbarth on Studio D productions in comparison with other NFB productions found that Studio D productions were borrowed or bought twice as often as other films produced by the National Film Board. We have an enormously successful studio, yet the President of the National Film Board is simply not giving it the opportunities it should have. This is despite its artistic success and popularity.
I believe my proposal is the only symbolic gesture I can make. I would like to see the NFB receive more money for Studio D and for other studios. However, I as a private Member cannot move for an increase in the budget. As all Hon. Members know, that is not open to a private Member. However, I am concerned that there be fairness for women and men film-makers. Women and men taxpayers contribute to the National Film Board and I am concerned about fairness.
As a parliamentarian, I am concerned that the head of an agency came before a parliamentary committee and gave an undertaking which he did not respect. I think we must respond to that, and I throw it back to the Government. What should the Government do when the word of the head of an agency cannot be relied upon? I believe that a person like that should be replaced with someone who will be honest and open to the


Supply
needs of Studio D and who will be fair to both the women and men who work at the National Film Board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today we have seen a perfect example of what would happen to government policies if the NDP ever got into power. We have heard a whole mish-mash of emotions but very few facts. Some of those facts, to be polite and use parliamentary terms, are so twisted that I cannot recognize from where they come from.
I would like to point out what the Eton. Member said in the exchange about the separate set-up for men and women at the National Film Board during the meeting of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture which the Hon. Member read. It reads:
I suggest to you that it is inadequate, that you are insensitive, and that you
have rested on the fact of having an employment equity program, which may
do great things in the long run.
The Hon. Member says that women have to run hat-in-hand and hat-pin in the other hand to react to men at the National Film Board. In saying that, she is omitting a few facts. The trustees of the National Film Board are composed of four men and four women. The National Film Board senior management committee is composed of three men and four women. The heads of the National Film Board's English regional studios are three men and two women. The National Film Board's French fiction studio which administers over $11 million in co-production funds is composed entirely of women. I do not know where she gets her figures.
I have before me the budget summary of the National Film Board for the period from 1983 to 1987. The figure at the bottom designates money attributed to the French unit of Studio D which our Government brought in, in 1986-87, first with a budget of $159,000 and now for 1987-88 a budget of $404,000. The Studio D budget went from $579,000 to $795,000, which means there is already $1,300,000 where there used to be $600,000 for Studio D and its French counterpart which did not exist previously. Added to that is the federal Women's Film Program, the International Year of Youth training project, which was also done by the NFB and dealt with men and women, the Employment Equity Program, which has $337,500 in training funds right now, as well as the Women's Market Development Group. In 1983-84, that was $504,142 altogether, and what is it for this year? It is $1,678,430. How can that be a decrease? I do not understand.
What we have here is a difference in philosophy. I have discussed with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-East (Ms. Mitchell) the NDP's approach to equality for women. Members of the NDP think in terms of quotas. Since 50 per cent of the people in Canada are women, they think that 50 per cent of every program everywhere, even if women are not involved in a particular activity, should be composed of women. That is ridiculous.
Members of the NDP think in terms of quotas and reverse discrimination. They think in terms of ghettos. They feel that if they cannot get their pound of flesh, men and women should
live in separate ghettos. That is the philosophy of the New Democratic Party. Members of the NDP think that women cannot hack it in the real world so they should be put in a favoured environment, watered and fed so that they will grow like beautiful flowers. That is nonsense.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I note that the Parliamentary Secretary simply totally ignored the Estimates of her own Department. She said she does not know where I got my facts. Expenditures in 1985-86 were $2,531,000, an amount which has gone down to $2,184,000 for 1987-88. I do not understand how that can be an increase. Of course, there has been a loss in purchasing power because of inflation. Those are the facts.
The Parliamentary Secretary has taken some very selective positions and has referred to them. The board of trustees does not decide which individual films will be funded. Let me quote what Mr. Macerola said about the NFB before the committee, and this can be found at page 42:36 of the transcript of the meeting of May 21, 1987. He said:
What I was saying is that for the time being, I am head of a cultural organization that is a male organization, like all the other ones. Therefore I have to redistribute the existing funds, that is I have to go and get the money that is being spent by male producers and directors in order to give it to another constituency.
He was complaining about my suggestion that Studio D ought to get more money. He said "no", that the NFB was a male organization, and that he had to cope with the male producers who run the NFB. That is what he said in committee. Then he went on to say:
The easiest way for me would be to "ghettoize" the women who work at NFB and increasing Studio D's budget by $2 million or $3 million.
He was counting on an increase to Studio D, which he promised before the parliamentary committee two years earlier. Then he said that that would be to ghettoize women.
It is absolutely preposterous to say that giving money to Studio D is to ghettoize women. If that is the policy of the Government, then it ought to get rid of Studio D altogether. We do not want a ghetto. We want a climate where women can work and get their stuff out. That is what Studio D was doing. I do not think the Government can have it both ways. If it wants to say that it is a ghetto, that it is a bad thing, then the Government ought to get rid of it.
We certainly cannot have the head of an agency come before a parliamentary committee in 1985 and promise an increase for Studio D, and then return to the same parliamentary committee two years later, having decreased the funds available to Studio D, with the excuse that it was on the grounds that the male producers who run the NFB would not let him do otherwise and that to give more money to Studio D would be to ghettoize it.
Why did he not say in 1985 that he was against Studio D and against ghettos? He has simply not been honest.


I should like to see the Parliamentary Secretary respond to these false statements made to the committee. I am absolutely astounded. She was not at the committee at that time, but now that 1 have brought it to her attention, I hope she will take it up with the Minister.
It is grossly irresponsible for her to say that it is all right for the president of an agency to come before a committee, to lie, to make promises and not to fulfil them, and then to attack someone who points that out and react personally. I think Parliament ought to be very concerned when the head of an agency comes before a parliamentary committee on the Estimates and lies before that committee.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I somewhat reluctantly join in this debate on Vote 60 in respect of the cut of $100,000 to the budget of the National Film Board.
Supply
I am disconcerted by the manner chosen by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) to bring to the attention of the House what she perceives to be untruths spoken and undertaken by the chairman of the board and our film commissioner in respect of Studio D.
I was not there in 1985. I was not the communications critic at that time. I was at part of the meeting to which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood referred in May, 1987.
1 actually left that meeting because I believe that one has an obligation to be at least polite and to maintain a degree of decorum when one is speaking with public servants and technocrats who are there to serve our society. One can disagree, but one does not have to be disagreeable. I was so discomfited that I left.
I went over the exchange but not with the same fine-tooth comb as the NDP Member went over the exchange. I have subsequently asked myself what we are talking about in respect of the National Film Board and women.
I know that the National Film Board has a very wonderful Studio D. I know that it produces some extraordinary films about, for, and addressed to women as well as the general population. The film commissioner has a commitment to the cultural space occupied by women at the National Film Board and to film-making in general, film-makers in Canada. He has been attacked by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood. In my view he has shown-and I say it in all sincerity- some leadership and a great deal of sensitivity to the matter of equal opportunity and to the development of women, not only in Studio D but throughout the National Film Board.
The track record of the National Film Board and the final results we have seen-and one must assume it is because of the leadership; I have no other way of making such a presumption-have indicated an ongoing improvement since the appointment of the present director, Mr. Macerola, in 1983. If we look at our other cultural industries, whether it is broadcasting, cable, television, or book publishing, in every single industry the situation of women and their presence in those industries is indeed something to criticize.
I suggest that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood is as strong a proponent of the role, space, and place of women as I am. However, I think we see things somewhat differently. I see the world as a shared partnership, families and people who live together in society. I do not look at 52 per cent per se. I look at competence, equivalents, and the right to move regardless of one's sex.
I also say that there has been discrimination and stereotyping and that therefore we must do some additional promotion, which is called employment equity. I have been very critical of the Government's employment equity Bill, Bill C-62. I have said very strongly to the Parliamentary Secretary-and she knows that I have said it-and to the Minister that all the right words are in place; the problem is that there are no teeth in the Bill to put employment equity into action. All one must do, according to the Government, is to deposit a report. You


Supply
can avoid any kind of punishment and any kind of sanction. That is not good enough, Madam Speaker. On that score, the Government has done lovely things with words, flowers and smoke and mirrors, but it has put no practical application to it. On the other hand, we have the chairman of the National Film Board, the film commissioner, who has said, contrary to all his other colleagues in the cultural field, "I intend to do something about this."
In December, 1986, the National Film Board announced- voluntarily-its plan to establish a new division to head an employment equity program which aims to achieve parity among women and men in all National Film Board staff and contract positions by 1996 and to ensure a more equitable place for women in all aspects of film-making in our society, particularly by establishing training and apprenticeship programs. I wish Treasury Board would take note of what the National Film Board has done and apply the same thing across all the Crown corporations in our Government. The goals set will be met through funding and hiring practices, through training programs, film crew selection procedures and greater support of the board's film unit.
The program is the first to be implemented by a major Canadian cultural organization. The program was initiated as a result of a study done by the National Film Board completed in November, 1986. It was not a surprise to me nor to the NFB that the study found that men make up 78 per cent of the management, 69 per cent of the film-makers and 85 per cent of the technicians. Furthermore, and I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary is well aware of this, men make $4,000 to $6,000 a year more than women in all categories except in the support staff. It is traditional and normal in Canadian society that women get paid a 60 cent dollar. I think women now get a 64 cent dollar, but we are looking for a 100 cent dollar.
In the meantime, the National Film Board took a really solid look at things. Because women comprised 72 per cent of the board's support staff and 93 per cent of the its clerical and secretarial staff it said something had to be done. In actual fact, when you look at the number of National Film Board employees, as of February 28, 1986, you have on full-time staff 324 women and 421 men. In terms of division, women are trying to get to an equal situation-we have not made it yet- but at least there is a program being put in place that will see an improvement in this unfortunate distribution which does not reflect women's competence, capabilities, ingenuity and creativity in the cultural sector. This program grew out of the Film Board's five year operational plan which guarantees Canadian women equal partnership in the National Film Board's reform.
The federal employment equity legislation to which I referred before, Bill C-62, passed last spring required all federally regulated employers and Crown corporations to report annually to Parliament on the progress in the hiring and
promoting of women, the disabled, native and visible minorities, as per the whole of Section 15 in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it being the equality section. The concept was to be applied in the National Film Board. We have been addressing particularly Studio D.
I suggest that there are other aspects which need to be addressed, not only Studio D, relating to visible minority women, relating to visible minorities, relating to native people, women, and native people in general. We have to look at the whole ball of wax and see what the National Film Board will come up with in all of these categories.
The Film Board, as you well know, Madam Speaker, does not fall under the employment equity legislation. That is why the President and his board must be complimented. They have shown leadership. They did not have to put themselves under Employment Equity legislation because NFB is an arm's length cultural institution. But Mr. Macerola intends to keep the Government informed about the progress and the implementation of the program. That is a very forward move.
The Member quoted from the hearings and the exchange with the Vice-Commissioner of the National Film Board, Joan Pennefather. I too asked about employment equity. She went on to tell us that not only was the NFB involved in an employment equity program, but it would also bring in contract compliance, something which the Government did not even bother to do in its legislation which it should have done and which was promised during the election. The Government forgot to keep that promise along with many others. What did Joan Pennefather say in response? She said that the National Film Board has gone further than the employment equity legislation and has implemented contract compliance. Contract compliance is an essential component of the employment equity program ensuring that when the National Film Board is working on co-ventures with partners in the independent producer sector, it will see that employment equity is involved through contract compliance.
The Hon. Member said there were cuts. There may have been some cuts. I am not prepared to argue down to the finest of details. But I am prepared to suggest that one should look at what happened to Studio D over a year ago. Through no fault of Studio D it had a deficit. Anyone who is in business, whether in public company business or private company business, knows that when you have a deficit it has to be dealt with. Studio D had to deal with that deficit. Studio D had a lot of carry-overs, projects which it carried over from 1985 to 1986. There was, and understandably so, some discontent at Studio D. There were film producers who were not getting jobs. There were new projects. Studio D has a million and one new ideas which are good, exciting and dynamic. But you and I know that we cannot have everything we want. We have to do things within certain parameters. Studio D, with this long list of carry-overs and with the deficit it had to pay back, did not have the kinds of funds it wanted that year.
Let us look at what has happened. Basically, we have had dollars invested in film projects produced and directed by


women. In the English branch we had a total of $18,121,898 in production, $6,581,334 of that or 36.3 per cent was done by women. In the French branch with a total of $12,334,697 of production, $3,610,423 or 29 per cent, was done by women. That is not fifty-fifty, but I hope we will move to fifty-fifty.
There have been no cuts in the over-all budget. In Studio D in 1983-84 they had $363,708, and the amount was $795,450 in 1987-88. I will place in the record, if I have time, the total of this budget, but I now want to go on to another aspect.
With respect to the over-all National Film Board, we are talking about five studios in Montreal, one in Toronto, one in Halifax, one in Winnipeg, one in Edmonton and one in Vancouver. Each one of these studios has projects dealing with women and with women's issues. Not all projects with respect to women come out of Studio D.
The Member said that she does not want to see Studio D perceived to be a ghetto, and neither do I. I am saying to you, Madam Speaker, and to the Member for Broadview- Greenwood, the leadership and the motion before us, which is a motion of censure on the management and leadership of Mr. Macerola, is not a fair critique. We see coming from all the studios some excellent projects and programs which deal with women and women's concerns. They are not just women's concerns, they are society's concerns. Things concerning women, from women's point of view, are very important. There are also women who produce and direct on their own, not necessarily in Studio D.
Studio D, which was founded in 1974, the International Year of Women, has produced many films to date. It has been a training ground for young film producers. They have gone on to other studios with their skills, training, their vision and view, scripts and productions.
Studio A is an animation studio and it boasts five studios in Montreal. It was founded by Norman MacLaren. Wendy Tilby of Vancouver has produced a wonderful film called Tables of Content. She has already won two major awards, one in France just last week. She won the best women's film award at the Annecy meeting in France. She does not come out of Studio D, she comes out of Studio A. Quite frankly, I do not care what studio she comes out of as long as she has produced a fine film with taxpayers' dollars which reflects women's concerns from a woman's perspective. I do not think she has to be from Studio D. Obviously, if Mr. Macerola were not interested in women, he would have done something that would have been counter-productive to producing these kind of women.
Studio A has an opportunities program for young children animators and film directors. On the French side, research is being done in the two-dimensional animation field. We have produced Sand Castle which won an academy award and gave us a chance to experiment in new technology and new technique.
Supply
In Studio B, the fiction studio, great features have been produced. We have had some excellent critical awards. One of the best film-makers, Donald Britton, did that film on Mackenzie King. Do not tell me that women in our society are not interested in Mackenzie King, his peccadilloes, his view of women and whether or not he looked in a crystal ball. Women are just as interested in that as men. The fact that it was produced in that studio does not detract from Studio B or the vision we have.
The film on Hal Banks which was produced last year had a very serious impact on the lives of women. It impacted on how their husbands live. I do not think you can discount that. Sitting in Limbo and 90 Days are excellent films that need to be recalled.
With respect to Studio C, the centre for documentaries, it has produced wonderful film series such as the one done by Gwynn Dyer on war and the consequences of war. Does that not impact on women? Some day we ought to look at a film series done by women on the impact and consequences of war. It might be a different film. I hope in that sense we will see an evolution in the role of women in the National Film Board. Co-production on the French side in that studio is very important.
In Studio G we are doing multi-media and educational programs. My friend talked about how young people view themselves within the educational framework. Those are important projects.
What is the true portrait? The NFB board of directors is composed of four men and four women. Senior management is composed of three men and four women. The heads of the regional studios are three men and two women. The French fiction Studio C, which administers over $11 million in coproduction, is composed of women only. What I am trying to say to you is that the NFB renewed its commitment to the federal Government's women's film program in the amount of $2 million over the next five years, and that is some commitment.
In closing I want to point out to you that the voice which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood brings to this debate is not consonant with the voices of some women's organizations. Madam Louise Dulude, in December, 1986, had only praise for the NFB announcement and said that since they are a federal government agency they are under no obligation with respect to employment equity or the promotion of women. She feels they deserve full credit. That credit goes to the head of the NFB. In March of 1987, MediaWatch, the Canadian Coalition Against Media Pornography, and the National Action Committee on the Status of Women held a conference called "Adjusting the Image: A National Conference on Canadian Broadcasting Policy" and paid compliments to the NFB.
I want to conclude by saying that I oppose the sense of the amendment. We cannot afford to cut $100,000 from the NFB. It goes against the creativity which has been demonstrated in


Supply
the leadership and all the way down the line. So 1 reject out of hand the amendment to the motion.

I am on page 42:36 of the minutes of May 21, 1987. He continued:

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to be able to say that I was there and heard it with my own ears. Regrettably, I had to leave before the end of the meeting. Therefore, I did not hear it. I have, however, read it. I wondered what the meaning of that jargon was. I called Mr. Macerola and asked him what he was talking about when he said: "I have chosen to enhance the cultural space occupied by women, not only within Studio D but also within the NFB and within the Canadian film-making milieu". I told him that I did not understand his philosophy in English and asked him to explain it to me.
I am glad the Member asked that question because the answer really meant that he was going to apply employment equity and ensure that women get equal opportunity based on their competence, the projects they will present, and the fact that they are creative, innovative and competent. subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity to speak to this particular motion. However, I must confess that it is not without a rather strong sense of incredulity that I find myself compelled to defend the proposed 1987-88 budget for the National Film Board. It is lamentable, in fact completely incomprehensible, that any Member of the House would suggest diminishing our support for the National Film Board of Canada.
As a member of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, I know I speak on behalf of all government Members in saying that the Government wishes it could have given more to the National Film Board this year and we regret the budgetary constraints that do not make this possible. However, we live in cognizance and awareness of certain economic realities.
I find it strange that a member of the Opposition would actually suggest that we appropriate less money for the National Film Board this year. I find it rather reprehensible that it would come from a Member who I believe has a long and distinguished record not only in the field of communications and culture, but in having women play a complete and equally participating role in Canadian society.


Supply
That Member has spent a great deal of her career defending the National Film Board and has often stated what she and the New Democratic Party believe are many of the dangers to culture from free trade. We know that these fears are unfounded. One has the impression of posturing when members of the NDP talk about a freer or enhanced trade threatening the cultural sovereignty of the National Film Board but then proposing less money for the National Film Board of Canada.
There is no question as to where the true danger lies. It is not with our Government's far-seeing policy of securing economic growth through expanding our markets. However, it is in the betrayal by any Member of the House of the kind of cultural rights that we try to uphold.
Many of us see these cultural rights residing in the National Film Board and the kind of work that it does. To undermine this cultural instrument in Canada through arbitrarily slashing money off the budget, $100,000 in this case, is truly dangerous to Canada's culture.
The Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), on this day when we discuss Estimates, should be defending the National Film Board rather than attacking it. Anyone versed in the cultural history of Canada would know that contribution that the National Film Board has made to our national identity. The international reputation of Canada has been indeed illustrious in the NFB's 48 years of history.
Established in 1939 by the legendary John Grierson, the board quickly became a pioneer in documentary film-making. It remains a world leader to this day.
In the early days when the NFB got its start, it did not remain exclusively in the documentary field for long. With the arrival of Norman MacLaren in 1941, the NFB began laying many of the foundations of its international reputation for imagination and innovation in the field of animation. This reputation still holds true today, not only for independent Canadian film-makers but in the good name of the NFB itself.
MacLaren was a genius who continually developed new film-making techniques, drawing, painting and even scratching directly on the film itself to achieve effects that others never even imagined. Norman MacLaren was honoured around the world not only for his artistic achievements, but also for his contribution to world peace and understanding through films such as Neighbours.
But his brilliance might never have been able to flower had it not been for the National Film Board, where he was free to transcend the commercial pressures of the bottom line and to pursue innovative ways that were artistically and culturally far ahead of many of the pioneer film-makers. His techniques have recently reached critical acclaim from mass audiences.
His productions, and those of the NFB in many disciplines-features, documentaries, shorts, animated films and videos-were far ahead of their time in the 1940s and 1950s. They were popular and acclaimed. In the ensuing 40 years,
NFB productions have appeared in some 60 languages and have won innumerable international film festival prizes, acclamations, and awards.
For example, in 1960, the film Universe won the Jury's Prize at the Cannes Films Festival for the exceptional quality of its animation, as well as 23 awards from other film festivals. Other NFB films have consistently won prizes at Cannes. These winners have included over the years: Blinkity Blank, City of Gold, Women on the March, and most recently all Canadians are very familiar and proud of Le Declin de I'Empire Americain which won the Cannes International Critics Prize just this last year.
Other NFB films have won the prestigious Robert J. Flaherty Award of the British Academy of Film and Television Arts. They include Nobody Waved Goodbye, Grierson, Los Canadienses, Prologue and Sad Song of Yellow Skin.
The films which were winners at Cannes and in the British Academy also won many other international prizes. However, these films represent only a few of the international award winning productions of the National Film Board of Canada.
Many Canadians, particularly those in the more widely distributed commercial film category, look to the American Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for the Academy Awards. The Academy Awards are often a test around the world of the commercial viability and success of popularly distributed film.
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has recognized the National Film Board achievements with an astounding total of over 50 Oscar nominations for NFB productions. The Film Board has had eight Oscar winners so far. They are: Churchill's Island in 1948, Neighbours in 1953, Le Chateau de Sable and I'll Find a Way in 1978, Special Delivery in 1979, Every Child in 1980, If You Love This Planet in 1982 and Flamenco at 5.15 in 1984.
All of these award-winning productions were rooted in the Canadian experience. Many involved powerful and occasionally searing explorations of Canadian cultural and social life.
Many were done on low budgets through the NFB's regional offices, which contracted much of the production work out to free-lancers.
We should all be very proud and amazed at what the NFB has accomplished with the money Canadians have entrusted to it over the years. The board's record calls for all the support that this Government is able to give to the NFB.
It is time for fiscal prudence. I believe every Canadian who sees the astonishing national debt that was bequeathed to this Government by years of reckless spending by previous Liberal Governments, knows that tough decisions must be taken to achieve the kinds of savings the Government needs.
The National Film Board has achieved substantial saving under its five-year plan. It is not a time to be lopping off $100,000 from the NFB budget, an institution which has been a source of great pride to many Canadians over the years.


I want to comment on this motion and why it has been moved at this time. Since it is not parliamentary to impute motives to another Member, I will not do so. Elowever, I will directly share with the Elouse why this is being done.
As a member of the parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, I know there has been a rather unfortunate, long-standing and ever increasing degree of enmity, animosity and open hostility between the New Democratic Party member of our committee, the Member for Broadview-Greenwood, and the very renowned and esteemed President of the National Film Board, Mr. Francois Macerola.
In a rather distasteful exchange recently before the committee, that NDP member called the President of the Film Board arrogant. Just this morning in committee, she said that he had "lied to the committee".
I understand that earlier this day during the debate the Member for Broadview-Greenwood also referred to iying. The Member's concern is about the place of women in the National Film Board and their place as producers and directors and those contributing to Canadian film. Her concern is shared by every Member of the House. They say the best way to make any man a feminist is to have daughters. That we will see our daughters with full equality with men in Canadian society in the next 10 or 20 years is of great importance to us.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext: That is paternalism.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60. DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
The Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party interrupted me just as I felt a wonderful speech on feminism coming, but perhaps I will save that for another day. We who have children want to see our daughters attain an equality in the arts, culture, business, law and in many other sectors of Canadian society.
The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood has had a long-standing row with the National Film Board over what she believes the NFB is doing in place of allocating funds for Studio D, the women's studio, for employment equity and for encouraging the development of women. However, I think the Hon. Member has far overstepped parliamentary privilege in referring to a Canadian citizen as lying under parliamentary privilege where that citizen has no recourse against that allegation. I think a careful examination of the record will show that as well as being unparliamentary and unfair, it is simply not correct in this case to refer to the film commissioner of Canada as having lied or having misled a parliamentary committee. More than that, this row has led to the motion today to eliminate $100,000 from the operating budget of the NFB. What the Hon. Member is trying to do is somehow to punish the film commissioner for what she believes has been a lack of performance on his part on behalf of women's issues.
The mind boggles at that philosophical approach. I do not always agree with Mr. Juneau of the CBC, but is the answer to cut more money from the CBC? I do not even like Knowlton
Supply
Nash. I would not have hired him as an anchor man. But should we eliminate his salary from the CBC? Any good and sensible parliamentarian would see that it is the height of irresponsibility to try to inflict upon a Canadian organization, particularly a cultural organization, one's own viewpoint, in this case, often dogmatically, by assaulting the fiscal planning of the NFB by trying to reduce money from its budget. I think Members of this House, particularly those on the government side, and members of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, feel a sense of revulsion about this.
I am not usually very partisan in this House, but this is really an example, I think, of what we see as a great contradiction. Back where I come from, the NDP goes out to talk to farmers and damns the grain handlers every time there is a strike. This is the same NDP which is run by the Canadian Fabour Congress, of which the grain handlers are dues payers. That is the height of hyprocrisy. It is typical of the New Democratic Party.
The NDP cultural critic, who extols the virtues of the NFB, as we all do, scares the devil out of the cultural community by saying the NFB will be jeopardized if we have free trade, and we all know that as false. Here is a person, who is a self-styled, well respected advocate of the NFB, standing in this House asking us to lop money from its budget. That cut in money is designed to cause personal harm to the Film Commission of Canada and the chairman of the NFB, Francois Macerola. I think it is a petty way to deal with one's difficulties and disagreements with the policy of the NFB.
I would hope that in the remaining part of this debate, and in the future of the NFB, we do not see this kind of narrowminded, overly partisan sort of attack, not only on the NFB but on the very integrity of a man who is respected by all Parties in this House for doing an excellent job in leading Canadian film policy. I would like to point out that if one looks at the record of NFB with respect to women, one will find that of the eight Oscar-winning films I mentioned just a moment ago, three have come from the NFB Studio D. The only permanent women's film making unit in the world, Studio D has often given compelling expression to the Canadian voice on the world's stage, a voice of conscience, reason and personal dignity.
Many who know my background will know I have not always agreed with Studio D. Some Studio D productions have offended my sense of balance on certain moral issues. However, do I, as a member of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, say to lop money from the budget of Studio D because I did not like a film on abortion, or that I did not like the direction taken in a certain program? All Members of this House know that that is not the way one tries to effect a balanced policy in Canada's National Film Board.
Not a Love Story, for example, which was nominated for an Academy Award in 1982, graphically portrayed the destructive effects of pornography on both men and women. This acclaim was given to the NFB for that production, and to


Studio D, wherein that production had its development and its promotion, and 1 think that was a very wide acclaim to us in Canada who are so concerned with the harmful effects of pornography. If You Love This Planet in many ways polarized and balkanized the great concern over how we view nuclear arms, and to all of us involved in the debate as parliamentarians, it gave us a warning and yet a hopeful message. I think that is something about which all Canadians are justifiably proud.
The continued support for Studio D is part of a comprehensive policy designed to increase the cultural space occupied by women.
During Francois Macerola's mandate, the NFB has increased resources to women working in studios and other parts of the country. Just recently a film on entrepreneurial women was shown to a meeting of Ministers for the Status of Women in Halifax. The NFB's over-all approach is to ensure fairness in the workplace for women. As the government film commissioner, Mr. Macerola, recently announced, an employment equity program, as detailed in Equality and Access a New Social Contract has been hailed as one of the most progressive anywhere in the federal Government. Mr. Macerola's action was not compelled or forced. This was voluntary. This was developed by a senior manager in Canada's Public Service who has that kind of commitment.
The NFB has undertaken to conduct a comprehensive program of employment equity as provided for in the Charter of Rights to improve the status of women not only in the employ of the NFB but in the film arts of Canada. The NFB has been reviewing its programming and distribution systems to ensure that all their components recognize and honour a commitment to the full partnership of women in Canadian society. It has identified specific training objectives to be pursued in terms of the promotion of women within its ranks.
I would think the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood, whose concern with the advancement of equality for women is well known to all Canadians, would want to reward Mr. Macerola for moving in the right direction. I know that until we have a House of Commons with 141 elected women- probably about 143 women would reflect the true percentage-women have some distance to go in Canadian society. But if one looks at the commitment of the NFB, at the testimony before the standing committee of Mr. Macerola and his senior staff, many of whom are very well respected women managers in the Public Service and in the film industry, I think one could take lessons in many respects from what the NFB has done. I would hope that as we analyse the NFB and its work, we would provide a hopeful message to the NFB, not only for the Studio D but particularly for women who are hoping to produce, write and make film across Canada, that these people can indeed be recognized as women and as Canadian artists in their own right.
For this reason, I will conclude by saying that I reject out of hand, as I am sure all Hon. Members do, that the NFB should have any kind of budget reduction based on a very partisan,
political aim, which I know is unacceptable to every Member of Parliament.

subsubtopic: POTENTIAL HAZARDS-CALL FOR CHANGES IN REGULATIONS AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today on Parliament Hill, Members of Parliament had the opportunity to meet with Cesar Chavez of the United Farm Workers who indicated his concern regarding the affect of pesticides on consumers and farm workers.
The control and use of pesticides are an issue of growing concern to many Canadians, and all New Democrats. Today the New Democrat environment critic in Alberta, John Younie, is launching a campaign to increase awareness of the potential hazards of many pesticides and calling on the federal and provincial Governments to implement the following changes to pesticide regulation and control: That Health and Welfare Canada, Environment Canada, and the general public should have more control over the registration of pesticides in Canada; that all substances in pesticides, including active and inert ingredients, should be listed on packaging and should be fully tested and registered; that stronger regulations on testing should be devised that ensure human and environmental safety, with the producer or distributor bearing the testing costs, and the use of all pesticides that do not meet test standards should be suspended until these standards are met; that the public should have access to all toxicological data concerning pesticides so that informed choices can be made regarding their use; and that a test review board should be established to permit an all-Canadian, independent audit of tests done by private labs to check the appropriateness, validity, methodology, lab practices and accuracy of test results.
These are measures which my New Democrat colleagues and I urge the Government to consider seriously.

subsubtopic: CHILE-CONCERN FOR SAFETY OF CARMEN QUINTANA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as of June 8, Carmen Quintana, the young Chilean student who was horribly burned with gasoline last July, returned to Santiago, Chile, to testify against the soldiers responsible for this hideous crime.
Quintana, who now resides in Canada, returned to Chile in April to meet with the Pope during his visit. While there, a death squad threatened to kill her, and written graffiti calling her a traitor were on walls everywhere. As a result of this previous visit, human rights groups in Chile and the InterChurch Committee for Human Rights in Latin America here in Canada are extremely concerned for her safety.
Carmen Quintana's lawyers, one of whom is from Montreal, are asking the Chilean court for an re-enactment of the incident that almost ended Carmen's life but claimed the life of a friend. The Pinochet regime has already conducted a reenactment but without the benefit of any witnesses.
The results of the Government's re-enactment show that Carmen kicked the container of gasoline on herself that nearly ended her life-a remarkable conclusion. Her lawyers are requesting another re-enactment with the benefit of witnesses to prove the Government's allegations to be incorrect.
It is clear that Carmen Quintana is in environment that is very hostile, and any requests to challenge the Pinochet Government's earlier claims of the incident will not be taken lightly.


I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to inform the Pinochet regime that the Canadian Government is maintaining a careful watch on Carmen Quintana throughout the trial until she returns to Canada, and to press other countries to pursue the same course.
