Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday of this week RCMP officials arrested six Toronto area immigration consultants and lawyers and charged them with aiding and abetting Portuguese nationals to remain in Canada through fraudulent means.
The role which certain unscrupulous lawyers and immigration consultants played in the movement of groups to Canada claiming refugee status is a matter of concern to us all. Such abuses bring our immigration laws into disrepute and, above all, have flooded our refugee determination system with false claims, while those refugees with valid claims have been forced to wait months and years before their claims could be resolved.
The Government's action in seeking out and charging individuals engaged in such reprehensible practices is to be applauded. I urge the Ministers responsible to continue their efforts to track down and prosecute those consultants and lawyers who prey upon the natural desire of people who, because of poor economic or political circumstances in their homeland, seek to come to Canada in the quest for a better life.

subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF INTRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure 1 rise today on behalf of all Saskatchewan Members of Parliament on both sides of the House. July 1 will be the twenty-fifth anniversary of the introduction of medical care into North America.
It was on July 1, 1962, that the first medical care plan came into effect in the Province of Saskatchewan. Tonight, community health care personnel from across Canada will have a special banquet to commemorate and celebrate that occasion in the city of Prince Albert. The guest speaker tonight will be the very distinguished Canadian, Mr. Emmett Hall.
The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) would normally want to make this statement, but he is currently making use of medical care. He is recovering from minor surgery, so he asked me to make the statement on his behalf.
On his behalf, and I am sure of all Saskatchewan Members of Parliament, I want to say that Canada owes a great debt of gratitude to the Premier of that day, Premier Woodrow Lloyd; to his Minister of Health, Mr. Allan Blakeney; to the former Premier of the province, the father of medicare, Tommy Douglas; and to Mr. Emmett Hall, who prefers to be called the grandfather of medical care.
Community health care workers who have gathered from across Canada in Prince Albert have asked me to request that pages distribute these little pins I hold here, commemorating this twenty-fifth anniversary, to all Members of Parliament from Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: APRIL TRADE SURPLUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the confidence of Canada's business and investment community continues to be reflected in sound economic figures. Not only are we hearing of a continuing decline in unemployment figures, increased new housing starts, and higher consumer spending, but Statistics Canada has reported that Canada posted a $1.6 billion merchandise trade surplus in April, the largest surplus since April, 1986.
The merchandise trade surplus-the amount that Canadian exports of wheat, metals, and other goods exceed imports- was up 55 per cent from the $1 billion level in March. Economists see the over-all April figures as a good sign for the Canadian economy.
My congratulations to Canadian producers for increasing their productivity and showing very clearly that Canadian producers can compete very favourably in world markets. This gives added impetus to our Government to secure an enhanced trade agreement.
1983 BUDGET-SPENDING PROJECTIONS

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 8, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) who was Acting Defence Minister for the day made a misleading and wrong statement in this House of Commons. The Minister's misleading statement was:
As a matter of fact the fiscal plan, and it is in the budgets of the former
Finance Minister, the Hon. Marc Lalonde, called for no increases in defence
spending after 1983.


Oral Questions
Then he went on to say:
I think the Hon. Member should check that out before making an accusation.
Imagine the Minister telling a Member of this House to check his facts when he hasn't even done so himself.
I have here the 1983 Budget Papers dealing with National Defence financing, Mr. Speaker. In the fiscal year 1983-84 the defence budget, under Marc Lalonde's fiscal plan, stood at $7,840 billion. In the next year an additional $930 million was added and in 1985-86 another $724 million was added. In 1986-87 another $865 million was added. In this present fiscal year another $766 million would have been added under the 1984 Budget, hence making it more than $800 million higher than the present Conservative Budget in this country.
Really the Budget Papers of 1983 and 1984 proved beyond a doubt, right here, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal defence spending projections called for sustained increases in the defence budget.
Meanwhile, we have the spectacle of two Conservative Defence Ministers running around the country trying to convince Canadians that they are doing such great things when, in fact, they are doing less than the previous Liberal Government whose defence purchases they are even trying to claim as their own. The program is a scam.

subsubtopic: REFORM OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE-PRIME MINISTER'S ACTIONS ON BEHALF OF CANADIAN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) leadership, Canada has been at the forefront of those nations calling for a new set of rules for international agricultural trade.
As a result of the Prime Minister's efforts, agriculture was raised as Canada's number one issue at the Tokyo Summit, the first time agriculture has been raised at a summit. Agriculture is being considered in the new round of GATT negotiations, and the OECD agreed to the need to reform international trade and issued a communique incorporating our Canadian proposal. One area of the Accord which needs vast improvement is its poor recognition of Canada's multicultural and aboriginal dimension which affects some 10 million Canadians.
Our Canadian society is undeniably made up of the French, English, aboriginal and multicultural dimensions. Clause 1 of the Accord only recognizes the English-French linguistic duality as a fundamental character of Canada. Therefore, is the Government prepared to amend and thereby strengthen Clause 1 by also entrenching the multicultural and aboriginal fact and reality as a fundamental characteristic of Canada so

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Youth and concerns the plight of unemployed and homeless youth. The Leader of the Official Opposition and myself met with representatives of various groups that are dedicated to helping unemployed and homeless youth. After explaining how upset they were about the Government's failure to act, they described the growing numbers of unemployed and homeless youth in Canada's main cities. There are between 10,000 and 20,000, depending on whether we are talking about Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver, while numbers are increasing in other Canadian cities. Mr. Speaker, these young people want to


Oral Questions
know why the Government has failed to take any concrete steps to deal with the plight of unemployed and homeless youth across Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth)):
subtopic: PLIGHT OF UNEMPLOYED AND HOMELESS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think we have to recognize there is a fundamental rule that applies to youth and their place in Canadian society, as far as employment and every other aspect of their lives is concerned. When the economy in Canada is not working properly, young people are the first to suffer, and when the economy picks up, they are the last ones called back. So for this Government, as I imagine it is for all other governments, the fundamental rule is to make sure the economy can function properly. That is why the youth unemployment rate has dropped 4.3 per cent since we came to power.
Second, I think the Hon. Member will agree there is no miracle solution to this particular problem. Recently, one of Canada's major newspapers published a series of articles on the homeless, and there were constant references to young people who in many cases suffered abuse from parents or other adults, in many cases, and young people who were victims of crimes and violence. These problems are not easily solved. However, we are very concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I think at least one thing is clear, and that is that homeless youth and the people who are responsible for helping them are amazed at all the pomp and circumstance with which some programs are launched, and I am sure that they would rather have something to put on their own dinner table. These young people would like to know whether the Government is truly concerned and, especially, whether it is prepared to put in place a permanent means of ensuring that someone will be giving their needs and their problems the attention they deserve.

I think it is excellent. I am a great supporter of the National Film Board. I have said publicly on many occasions that 1 think it ought to have more money.
My concern in my resolution is apropos a very specific question, that is, the refusal to give an increase to Studio D, which was promised at a previous committee meeting.
I am pleased to see the support for the NFB and Studio D given by the Hon. Member. I note that at committee he was not at all supportive of Studio D. As reported in the committee hearing for May 21, he said:
I watch sometimes with dismay ... Studio D, for example, very dogmatic. It is the work of ideologues, some of it, and very sadly. I do not find much of an appeal-in fact, I find it rather offensive.
Then the head of the NFB pointed out that nevertheless it made a certain amount of money, that the returns were good. The Hon. Member was rather surprised by this; he was not a supporter of Studio D at all. I am simply interested that he has changed his tune.
1 have a very specific question to ask him. It concerns the statements made by the head of the NFB on May 9, 1985. He indicated:
It will be a significant and a very important increase-
He was referring to the budget of Studio D, and those are his words. How can the Hon. Member for The Battlefords- Meadow Lake reconcile a promise of a significant and a very important increase in funding for Studio D with the figures in the Estimates?
The Government's own Estimates for 1985-86 indicate $2,531,000 for production and $288,000 for marketing. For the following year, 1986-87, there was a decrease to


$1,908,000 for production and an increase in marketing to $273,000. For the following year, 1987-88, there is $2,184,000 for production and $228,000 for marketing. That is clearly a decrease. However, the resources for that section, English language production, had increased from $22,960,000 to $24,939,000.
How does the Hon. Member reconcile these figures with the statement made in committee that there would be a significant and a very important increase?

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60, DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the way in which Parliament and its committees work makes it very difficult for Members who do not serve on a committee, such as the one with which we are dealing today, to be as knowledgeable and as aware about the actual workings of, in this case, the National Film Board as one would like to.
1 enter this debate because I have been very interested, supportive and impressed by the tremendous work which the National Film Board has done over the years, beginning during the World War II years when it was organized and led by John Grierson and by many of the people whom I have known, some who came from my City of Winnipeg, such as Gordon Burwash and later Bernard Ostry.
We know that films made by the National Film Board dealt with every aspect of Canadian life, even labour management relationships. We saw recently the film the NFB produced about Bob White, head of the Canadian Autoworkers Union. It has dealt with farm problems, with inner-core city problems, and with the problem of racial prejudice.
I remember a film made many years ago which dealt with prejudice and discrimination against black people who at that time lived in Dresden, Ontario, whose grandparents and great-parents came from the United States before and during the Civil War because Dresden was the end of the underground railway for slaves escaping from the U.S. We know how many awards and on how many occasions in national and international competitions at film festivals the National Film Board has been honoured.
We know that at the National Film Board, as at the CBC and in the private film and TV industries, many more women are now involved than there were some years ago. That does not mean we are satisfied that women have yet achieved the important role which they ought to play at the National Film Board or anywhere else.
Let me say something about the whole question of employment equity, not just at the NFB but everywhere. I had the opportunity to spend about 15 years of my life before I came to Parliament and after coming here working with the Canadian Labour Congress on the whole question of the kind of prejudice and discrimination which we had and still have- hopefully to a lesser degree-in this country against people who are non-white, against women, against natives and against handicapped people. It was the labour movement in cooperation with farm groups, co-operatives and church groups which persuaded first the provinces and then the federal Government to enact the fair employment practices Act and the fair accommodation practices Act and later the Bill of Rights.
We have accomplished a great deal, but we have a long way to go. I want to say to the Parliamentary Secretary that one of
the very sad things so far as we are concerned is that the employment equity legislation which the Conservative Government is so proud of is flawed. If you compare the Act here and the way it is in the legislation in the United States, Madam Speaker, you will see very quickly that our legislation is very much the way President Reagan would like the American legislation to operate. In other words, our legislation is based on voluntary compliance. That will not work. In the United States where the Americans have had a great deal more experience than we have had with that kind of legislation, the U.S. Manufacturers' Association has said that it is quite happy with the laws as they are. The U.S. law gives them a target. It tells them that they have to move toward hiring more people from minority groups: the non-whites, the handicapped and women. Companies are given goals. A year later they have to report how far they have moved to accomplish the objectives given. There are no misunderstandings, nor misapprehensions.
If you leave things loose and to voluntary acceptance, there will be criticism because there will be something that has not been done that should have been done. Unfortunately, this Government did not take the time to look into the way the system works in the United States and it is following an entirely different course which, as I pointed out, even the Manufacturers' Association in the U.S. says will not work. It will not work in the States and it will not work in Canada.
Having said that, I want to deal with the National Film Board. As I have said, and I have said it many times both in the House over the years that I have been here and in committee when I was a member of that committee, we are happy with the work done by the National Film Board. We would support any proposal by this Government, as we did for the former Government, to increase the budget of the National Film Board to permit and encourage the National Film Board to do even more than it has done. We know at the NFB as everywhere else there are not enough women, certainly not in responsible positions. There are still not enough people employed at the NFB who come from the visible minorities. There are still not enough people who are physically handicapped. That is true of every government Department and agency. It is true of every private sector employer. We want that situation to change. We do not call for quotas, but what we do say is necessary is some reverse discrimination.
Minority groups, whether women, handicapped, ethnic groups or non-white groups are represented in the NFB as in every other employment in this country, but they are underrepresented. We do not say, "Hire them just because they are women, handicapped, from visible minorities or are native", but we say, "If they have the qualifications to do the job for which there is a vacancy, then give them a little bit of extra support, because unless you do, we are probably looking at 100 years before they will get their fair share." We are not saying we want precise quotas. We are saying we have to make a special effort, and I do not see that being done by the Government.


I want to say something about the National Film Board and the work it has done for women. We in Manitoba are very proud of the fact that the NFB produced in my City of Winnipeg a series entitled Daughters of the Country. It consisted of four one-hour dramatic episodes. I am proud of the NFB for doing it and I am proud of the NDP Government of Manitoba which helped make the series possible by investing $500,000 in the project through its jobs fund. That was an important series because it depicted the history of the Metis people as seen through the eyes of Metis women. We hope there can be more series like that and we hope to see a great deal more film productions by the NFB in the regions. Whether it be in the Maritimes, the Prairies, or British Columbia, we want to see a lot more of it.
Let me say a word about Studio D. We know it has produced some excellent films. We know it could do more. We have to, as I have over the years, support and defend the CBC and call for more assistance. I have done that even though not infrequently I see a CBC program I disagree with. I expect the same will be true of the NFB. I want the film board to do more. I want it to give women more opportunities. I would be concerned if any Member of Parliament started to interfere with the work the NFB does on specific projects.
I am reminded of the film it made about Billy Bishop. I saw the film, but I must admit I am not an expert on Canadian history, and even less of an expert on Canadian military history. I do not know whether it gave an accurate depiction of Billy Bishop and his involvement in World War I. However, it really disturbed me when Members of the other place made what I considered to be a very vicious attack on the NFB. I hope we let the NFB do its job. If we are not satisfied with the way the board treats Studio D or some other group, that can be discussed in committee, as it should be.
Aside from that, I think on the whole we have a great deal to be grateful for to the NFB for what it has done over the years. I am looking forward to many more great productions and I urge the Government not only to give the support it has up until now to the NFB, but to increase its funding and let it do an even better job in future.

I would like to tell him about how the responsibilities of the Minister for the NFB are defined. This will show that the Hon. It has never been interpreted to mean that the Government becomes involved in the day-to-day operational

Today we are being asked in this motion to subtract $100,000 from the NFB budget. That amount bears a curiously strong relationship to the salary of the chairman of the NFB. Madam Speaker, let me answer that question by relating to the Hon. Member the answer I gave to someone after a two-hour discussion on the question of capital punishment. This person is a member of my Party in my constituency and he disagreed with me very violently on this question. When I realized after two hours that I could not convince him that abolition was a good idea, and I knew very well that he would never convince me that I should support capital punishment, I tried to think of a way to get out of this pointless discussion without offending him too much. I told him that we would never agree on the subject of capital punishment but there was one thing I thought we could agree on. That is, this is a wonderful country because he had stopped his Member of Parliament for two hours, called him all sorts of names and told him how wrong he was, but he knew and I knew that if he went home that evening he would not be fired from his job. subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1987-88-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 60, DEPARTMENT OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure Hon. Members will not be surprised to hear that the Government stands behind the Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1988, as tabled on March 2 of this year. Indeed, 1 find it hard to understand why the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) would propose a reduction in funding for an organization which has contributed so much to Canada's cultural development and which has been particularly responsive to the interests and concerns of Canadian women. Were it possible in the current climate of fiscal austerity, the Government would happily increase funding to the National Film Board of Canada, a fine organization of which all Canadians can be proud.
Hon. Members are well aware of the enviable reputation of the National Film Board of Canada. From its founding in 1939, the NFB has built a record both at home and abroad as a producer of films of the highest artistic quality in all areas; features, documentaries, shorts, animated films and videos. More than almost any other institution in Canada, the NFB
has allowed Canadian men and women to capture their own cultural identity, to perceive more clearly who and what they are, and to reach a fuller comprehension of the values that shape and define the society in which we live.
Each year, this year being no exception, a number of films produced by the NFB enjoy acclaim both in Canada and abroad. Permit me to cite some statistics from the 1986-87 fiscal year alone. During that period, 146 NFB films obtained prizes; 69 in Canada, 40 in the United States, 30 in Europe and one in Australia. Of these 146 prizes, 57 were awarded to fiction films, 50 to documentaries, 30 to animation films, three to film strips, and six to special projects.
1 imagine many Members have seen a film called The Decline of the American Empire, which was co-produced by the National Film Board. It garnered 18 awards, including the Silver Hugo in Chicago and the International Critics Prize at the Cannes Film Festival. It was the first Canadian film ever to receive an Oscar nomination as the best foreign film. It was voted best foreign film by the New York Film Critics' Circle.
I would like to mention a few of the other titles which have received honours and awards. They include Canada's Sweetheart, the saga of Hal C. Banks, Democracy on Trial, Final Offer, Sitting in Limbo, Sonia and The Big Snit.
I should point out, Madam Speaker, that the NFB continued to earn awards, critical acclaim, and wider audiences for its films despite a reduced budget. Like other departments of Government, the NFB has had to contribute its share to cost-cutting in keeping the Government's deficit within reasonable limits. From April, 1984, to April, 1986, the NFB's permanent staff was reduced by 25 per cent, from 947 to 705.
Savings resulting from the reduction of permanent staff and administrative costs were intended to generate more funds for the production and distribution of films and videos. However, cumulative vote reduction in the order of $5.5 million from 1984-85 to the present hampered the NFB's ability to realize these objectives. Yet, today we hear the unusual proposition by the NDP Member of Parliament for Broadview-Greenwood that the budget be further reduced by $100,000.
In addition to its artistic achievements, the NFB places a high priority on contributing to the development and advancement of film technology to the benefit of the film industry as a whole. For example, the NFB contributed to the perfection of the Imax three-dimensional camera and to the making of the first genuinely three-dimensional visual document. This work, called Transactions, was one of the major events at Expo 86 in Vancouver where it attracted 1,700,000 visitors from every corner of North America and the world.
Research and development are being carried out on several fronts simultaneously. Revolutionary new technologies such as computer assisted animation, infography, and many other techniques are being developed in NFB studios.
In co-operation with the private film sector and with university research centres, the National Film Board is

working in the field of videodisc, high definition television, stereophony and electronic editing. The NFB remains on the leading edge of new technologies, developing them for its own purposes as well as making them available in Canada and abroad.
The National Film Board takes a dynamic approach to communicating with its audience, an approach which allows it to reach more Canadians and to increase continually its presence on national television during prime time as well as on educational channels. As an example, in 1985-86 audiences for National Film Board productions scheduled during prime time on the French and English national networks increased by 54 per cent respectively over the previous year. Furthermore, the National Film Board has been able to successfully market many of its films abroad. Members of the public who watch PBS stations in the United States can see many National Film Board productions.
The NFB also takes seriously its role in the community and the importance of producing films which can lead to the betterment of life for Canadians. In this context, I want to point to a specific program of video productions aimed at warning children about the serious problems of sexual abuse. The distribution of this series called Feeling Yes, Feeling No, in English and French, is being handled by public organizations across Canada in connection with the NFB.
The latest report indicates sales of some 7,686 copies of these videos in the past few months. Following an agreement reached between the National Film Board and Health and Welfare Canada, 3,500 video cassettes in French and English will be distributed soon in public libraries across the country.
The National Film Board has also taken initiatives to broaden the audience for its films through agreements with public and school libraries. The agreement concluded with the Public Library at Quebec City is a noteworthy example of the validity of this approach.
During the 1984-85 fiscal year, before the agreement was signed, the Quebec Public Library had rented 335 video cassettes and screened 254 on its premises. After the agreement was signed, during the 1985-86 fiscal year, 5,525 video cassettes were rented from the library. In the first nine months of the following fiscal year, the number of rentals rose to 8,070, in addition to 3,700 inside screenings. This means that in less than two years, rentals and screenings in total rose from 500 to 10,000. "
Let me turn for a moment to the specific concerns which the Member for Broadview-Greenwood has expressed over the position of women at the NFB. As Hon. Members may be aware, in 1974 the National Film Board created Studio B, a separate unit within the NFB designed to meet the particular needs of women film-makers and audiences.
Since its creation, Studio D has earned an international reputation for producing unique and often controversial films.
Supply
Its productions include Not A Love Story, an award-winning film on the pornography industry's exploitation of women. They also include If You Love This Planet, an academy award-winning film about nuclear war.
Studio D is unique in the world as a film production unit directed by women producing films by, for and about women. Its mandate is to provide training for women, with emphasis on the film crafts from which women have been traditionally excluded, to increase the employment of professional women film-makers across Canada, to maintain an environment where women can bring women's perspectives to all social issues through the medium of film.
Since its inception, Studio D has produced, co-produced or assisted in the production of approximately 80 films. These included films made under the Federal Women's Film Program, those made under the International Youth Year Training Project Film, the Working Mothers series and the Canadian Children's series.
Studio D was responsible for the creation of the Federal Women's Film Program in 1981. This program is aimed at increasing the number of informational, educational and promotional films produced by, about and for women, as well as increasing opportunities for the creative expression of women. The Federal Women's Film Program produces and distributes films and organizes information campaigns and workshops.
Recently, the Canadian Institute for the Promotion of Culture for Women declared Studio D a "national treasure". Kathleen Shannon, Director of Studio D from 1974 to 1986, received the Order of Canada for her contribution to filmmaking in Canada.
In November, 1986, the NFB announced the creation within the French program branch of a women's production unit. This unit's mandate is to increase the presence and influence of women in all areas of documentary film-making within the French program branch. This unit will strive to promote discussion and change in social, cultural, economic and political relationships between men and women, and focus on new ways of examining human relationships.
The creation of Studio F is just another example of the commitment by the National Film Board to expanding the role of women in Canadian film production.
In December, 1986, the National Film Board announced plans to begin implementing, early in 1987, an employment equity program designed to increase the participation of women in film production and ensure that women achieve parity with men in all NFB staff and contract positions by 1996. The Hon. Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) has expressed her enthusiastic support for the NFB's employment equity program, which is one of the most extensive in any government agency.
All areas of the NFB's recruitment, training, promotion and contracting practices will be addressed in order to ensure that


Supply
women achieve parity in what is generally still a male-dominated industry. For example, in competition with all other factors being equal, preference will be given to hiring women in occupations where they are under represented. At the NFB, these include management positions as well as positions as film directors, producers and technicians. Conversely, men will be given identical preference in occupations where they are under represented. The only occupation at the NFB where men are under represented is support staff, particularly secretarial and clerical jobs.
This program is based on targets and timetables established by managers, and parity is to be achieved through funding and hiring practices, training programs, film crew selection and procedures, and the sustained support of Studio D and Studio F.
While the NFB maintained a voluntary equal opportunity program, the mandatory employment equity program was established to address inequities that have persisted within the NFB and in the film industry in general.
The chairman of the National Film Board recently told the House of Commons Standing Committee on Communications and Culture:
Despite the progress we have recorded and the success we have achieved, it is increasingly difficult for us to provide the material and financial support necessary for a more dynamic development of three production sectors in particular which are vital for the social-cultural equilibrium of Canadian cinema: production of films by women, regional production, and the production of feature films developed from alternative models.
In other words, a cut in the Estimates for the National Film Board would likely result in cuts to production of films by women, and I cannot believe that this is a result which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood would wish to see.
Rather than entertain the Hon. Member's motion to reduce the NFB's funding by a further $100,000, I suggest that the House reaffirm its support for this excellent Canadian institution. In particular, I suggest that we reaffirm our support for the Board's continuing efforts to ensure the fullest possible participation of women in one of Canada's most important cultural industries.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to put some comments on the record regarding this particular motion by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I believe it is important that Members realize what is happening here today.
We have heard many accusations from Hon. Members which I suspect were made with honourable intention. There were suggestions that the New Democrats wanted to see a decrease in the federal support for the National Film Board. Nothing could be further from the truth or more distant from reality. Nothing could be more illogical in relation to what New Democrats have stood for since their inception.
For decades and decades we have been on record on every occasion as recognizing the value of the National Film Board in terms of the strategic role it plays in bringing Canadians together, making us proud of our culture and heritage and recognizing the past achievements of outstanding Canadians. We would like to see the budget for the NFB increased. That is why we are so outraged today when we look at the Estimates before us and see that the significant increases which have been called for by all Canadians have simply not occurred. Once again the NFB, for all intents and purposes, when one factors in the rate of inflation, has fallen under the axe, the knife and chain-saw of the hackers in the Department of Finance when it comes to budgeting.
Let us for once indicate the truthful position. We want to see a significant increase in the funding of the NFB in all areas. 1 want to focus on one area in particular, and that is the area about which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood made her comments and what precipitated this particular vote. The Hon. Member was concerned about one of the critical areas of the NFB, referred to as Studio D, which is particularly involved with the production of movies, videos and other forms of communication, portrays the concerns of women and develops the talents of women in film production and in a whole variety of other very crucial areas. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood raised this particular issue of Studio D in committee. She put to the president of the National Film Board a variety of questions to find out from his perspective what was going to happen to the funding for this particular sector of the NFB. He said that the objective is to increase the budget of Studio D and to increase the amount of money devoted to film making by women at the NFB. He said it would be a significant and very important increase.

We can debate which are the most critical areas in terms of support for film production of the NFB, but when it comes to women's issues and children's issues, I certainly feel these are areas which ought to receive a considerable expansion of funds as opposed to a reduction of funds. Under no circumstances are we suggesting that the over-all budget of the National Film Board should be dramatically decreased now or in the future. It is exactly the opposite. We are advocating a significant increase in the funding for the National Film Board.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood was simply trying to make an important symbolic gesture to the President of the National Film Board to the effect that when he appears before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture and says to its members that it is his intention to significantly increase the budget for Studio D and women's programming, and a number of other areas which I will not take the time to mention, that that is what we assume he means. But when he obviously agrees and then in the final budget analysis does something different, we want to register our concern with that decision.
The National Film Board is something about which we feel very strongly. As a matter of fact, as a youngster going to school 1 remember those Friday afternoons when we watched films about Canada. It was probably a way for us to run out the week and give the teachers a bit of a break, I suppose, since we were restless on Friday afternoons. But year after year I was introduced to parts of Canada through the National Film Board. I became educated and informed as to the lifestyle and culture of people living in Labrador, parts of Newfoundland and northern Quebec-in fact, all parts of Canada. For that, to this day, I am very grateful.
I certainly wish to recognize the outstanding contribution that the National Film Board has made to international cinema. The awards which it has won in virtually every film festival has put Canada, along with a number of other private producers, on the cinema map of the world. For that we are all grateful.
I simply wish to clarify these two points. The first point is our support for the National Film Board funding. The second is with respect to the concern of the president in terms of what appears to be his commitment to increasing significantly the amount of money for women's productions under NFB.

Madam Speaker, of course the subject I want to discuss this afternoon is whether the RCMP, as a federal agency, realizes that the Official Languages Act applies to all federal agencies, including the RCMP.
Madam Speaker, there are problems in certain agencies, and today I would like to take this opportunity to discuss these and perhaps even try and correct some of the problems that exist at the RCMP.

Madam Speaker, there was a time when public opinion in this country was such that it was very difficult to introduce bilingualism in the public service in general and especially in certain Government agencies.
Today, although some reluctance still exists, I have the feeling, and I think the House will agree, that in our Canadian federation we are seeing a phenomenon that is the exact opposite of what we saw nearly twenty years ago in 1969, when the Official Languages Act was adopted. Today, we see in this country an increasing understanding, respect and generosity within the language groups and as a result, I think we have a far better understanding between the founding groups. Canada's duality is in better shape today.
As I said, attitudes have changed and the public at large has become ever more aware of this reality, acknowledging as well that it is necessary for the federal Government, its agencies included, to ensure full respect for this legislation, the Official Languages Act, and to promote it among Canadians generally.
The situation, Madam Speaker, more specifically with respect to the RCMP, is not particularly encouraging, something we have been witnessing for several months both in committee and in the House. RCMP officers are complaining, they write letters, and I could quote lengthy passages of the letter written and made public by C Division Assistant Commissioner J.E.J. Julien, an important letter which indeed raised a few eyebrows and bore the signature of many people, among others that of the C Division Assistant Commissioner, and which I think reflected the state of mind in Quebec.
In the rest of Canada, particularly here in the national capital, we could tell that the central administration was somewhat ill at ease.
At times it was difficult to make the RCMP Commissioner admit, in committee and elsewhere, that he was in the process of attempting to convince the force to show respect and follow the three major themes: the main theme being the language of service, that is the language of the institution which must serve the Canadian public; the language of work, of course, which is the right of every Canadian individual to work in the language of his or her choice, be it English in Quebec or French elsewhere, a worthy objective; and the third theme, which is fair representation.
Generally speaking, I think we have now reached what might be called an equitable level of about 26 or 27 per cent within the Public Service of Canada, and I am pleased about that.
However, I found it rather strange to hear and read that the RCMP was talking about reducing its objective, which was not 26 or 27 per cent, but 20 per cent, and which it had set in agreement with government authorities a few years ago, to some 12 or 14 per cent of the regular force, and this is why I would like to examine these events chronologically. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a couple of points to make. I participated in the Official Languages Committee when this subject was covered. It is difficult not to support the concept put forward by the previous speaker. The dilemma, of course, is that everyone in the House asks that Parliament be respected and that linguistic fairness and the targets outlined by the Parliament of Canada be respected by not only the RCMP but by all other agencies in the country. So we completely support that principle. We regret that the RCMP has not been able to move in a more satisfactory manner toward linguistic equality.
Back in the early 1980s we saw a period of time in which the country was in a deep recession. At that time very few people left the RCMP and recruitment was very low. Indeed, the Government of the day provided very few resources to enable the RCMP to meet its targets. Unfortunately, the RCMP did recruit quite a number of Francophones during this period of
time to the exclusion of many other areas that had to be addressed.
It was pointed out in the committee, and has been pointed out in the country over the past few years, that the RCMP functions primarily in western Canada and in the North. Many Anglophones who had exceptionally good qualifications were denied access to the RCMP while the organization tried to meet its linguistic commitments in a period of very low recruitment.
One must come back to the Government of the day in that period from 1980 to 1984 and ask this. Why were additional resources not put aside so that the RCMP could meet its targets? Why was it not insisted upon that special resources be put aside to recruit and to meet those targets?
The same Government deprived the RCMP of resources to meet other important areas. The RCMP functions in native communities. It provides law enforcement services to native communities in the North and in the western provinces. What we have here is a very serious under representation of native people and of women. The RCMP provides law enforcement in areas in which I think it is absolutely important that the number of women officers be increased. The force deals with issues such as sexual abuse of children and rape and assault.
It is a situation in which the proportion of women for effective law enforcement be increased for two reasons. The first is that in many cases they deal more effectively in that area of offences. The second is that in terms of striking some form of fairness and equality for the participation of women that more initiative has to be put into recruiting women for the RCMP. Indeed, in these years I personally raised matters with officials of the RCMP because in the area of the country I represent there is a desperate need for women members, both with respect to the point of equality and with respect to their ability to deal more effectively in some areas of law enforcement.
We have lost the initiative in three important areas because the Government of the day failed to provide the resources to the RCMP in periods of low recruitment to make those programs work. Indeed, the same kind of shortage of resources is presented today in the Budget of the present Government. The present Government has turned a blind eye to the issue of allowing the RCMP to meet those targets with additional resources, especially with respect to these primary and important areas: increasing linguistic equality and the recruiting of more women and native people so that they can be present in the communities in which the RCMP provide law enforcement services.
I for one support the principle put forward by my colleague who serves on the Official Languages Committee in a very distinguished and effective manner. This point must be addressed and we support it, but we must not lose sight of the need to recruit more women and native people into the RCMP.


Certainly the issue of multicultural representation is critical as well. The Government of the day must provide resources to meet the targets and it must provide resources that are specifically targeted to aid in that area of recruitment.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to respond to that. I think there are grounds for the kind of grievance expressed, particularly by western Canadians. I for one believe that there have been some errors in balancing recruitment over the years, and it goes both ways.
In his comments to the committee, Commissioner Simmonds recognized that indeed the RCMP is a national force and it must recruit nationally, but it must also meet its provincial contract requirements and accept the fact that a large portion of the force is mobile. Many members of the force are called upon to spend two or three years in one place and then have to move either because of the requirements of the force, because of experience or sometimes because of promotions. I accept that. I think over the years there has been some imbalance, but in the last few years the recruitment of Francophones and Anglophones has been pretty well equal to proportional population representation and of course to the workload of the force.
I am told that in 1983-84, 65 per cent of the only 84 members who were recruited were Francophones. Of course, there were only 84 members recruited that year because there was a down-sizing of the force. In the last year, there were 542 recruits and 26 per cent of those were Francophones. There has been a re-establishment of the proportions.
I understand the grievance of the western provinces. I understand they feel that they should be well represented, and I accept that. However, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, we have a long way to go to ensure regional representation and allow both the English-speaking in Quebec and the Francophones outside Quebec to participate fully in this national public service. We understand the difficulty. The grievance is well put and we will try to work toward reestablishing some equity.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN VOTE 25, DEPARTMENT OF THE SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) opposing the $662,941 operating expenditures proposed in the RCMP Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1988. Given the Hon. Member's longstanding interest in official languages issues and particularly in those matters pertaining to the official languages program of the RCMP, I would like to take this opportunity to provide to the Hon. Member and other Hon. Members some indication of the current status of official languages in the RCMP and of the direction the force will be going in the future.
A balanced assessment of the RCMP with respect to official languages will recognize both accomplishments as well as areas where continued efforts are required. With respect to
Supply
accomplishments, the force has been highly successful in developing innovative approaches to delivering bilingual policing services to the public in the vast unilingual areas served by the RCMP through the use of the unit bilingual complement concept.
The unit bilingual complement, or UBC, approach ensures that in each of the 276 significant demand areas served by the force, at least one officer is available to provide the public with bilingual service. Approximately 90 per cent of all UBCs are fully staffed with competent bilingual personnel. Efforts are continuing to improve practices so that the public is aware that service is available in both languages in these predominantly unilingual regions of Canada.
In bilingual regions such as northern Ontario, New Brunswick and the metropolitan areas of Quebec where both official languages groups represent a sizeable portion of the population, well over 80 per cent of serving RCMP members are bilingual. These figures reflect a significant commitment by the RCMP to offering, where required, service to the public in both official languages.
I am of course aware that the Government's official languages program consists of more than just service to the public. It also seeks to improve the language of work environment and to provide for equitable participation of both language groups. The status of these other aspects of the official languages program of the RCMP has experienced a gradual but sustained improvement over the last decade. I use the word "gradual" advisedly as incremental change is the only type of change possible in a career organization such as the RCMP. This is particularly so when it pertains to changes to the profile of RCMP members themselves.
Francophone participation in the RCMP stood at approximately 9.8 per cent in 1976 when the official languages program was first established. Since that year, the RCMP, through a vigorous recruitment program in which bilingual skills were given a very high priority, has increased the number of Francophones on average by 0.5 per cent per year. These results were achieved as a direct result of RCMP recruitment efforts and are evidence of the force's commitment in this area.
I should also add that in addition to recruitment, another reason for the advances made by the RCMP in increasing its bilingual resources and Francophone participation has been language training. The recruit official language training program was introduced in 1977, and since commencement, over 400 unilingual recruits, equitably divided between English and French-speaking candidates, have been given training in the other official language.
Having referred to areas in which the RCMP has made substantive progress, including the development and implementation of the UBC concept in unilingual areas, a proactive and progressive recruitment program designed to support official languages objectives and a small but effective cadet language training program, I will now touch upon three areas where further work is necessary.


Supply
The Commissioner of Official Languages has commented upon the number of bilingually designated positions in the RCMP in which the incumbent does not yet fully meet the language requirements of the position. In headquarters, for example, just over 50 per cent of bilingual positions are staffed by members who do not meet the linguistic requirements of the position. This can, of course, be explained by the fact that headquarters is made up of members drawn from the regions, most of whom served in English-speaking provinces. Nevertheless, this points to the need for the force to increase beyond its immediate requirements the size of its bilingual resources. A substantial pool of bilingual members is necessary if the force is to maintain a flexible policy of promotions and transfers while at the same time maintaining a high level of bilingual capability at headquarters.
It might also be stated that the Francophone participation rate is both a success and a shortcoming. It is a success in comparison to where the force was in the past but a shortcoming in view of where it wants to be in the future. Francophone members of the force still comprise less than 15 per cent of the regular member category, exclusive of special constables, a considerable distance from the full participation objective of 20.8 per cent for Francophones which the force set for itself in 1978.
These and other shortcomings have been referred to by the Commissioner of Official Languages and by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier during committee hearings on official languages. As the Hon. Member is aware, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) has submitted proposals to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) for changing some aspects of the RCMP official languages program.
These proposals are designed to address the shortcomings which I have just mentioned. It is also worth noting that these proposals would build on the successes of the existing official languages program.
I am speaking here of the UBC concept which has been demonstrated as being a flexible and valid approach to providing bilingual service in unilingual areas. I am also referring to the recruit official language training program, and I believe that I can safely say at this point that there will be no dimunition at this time to the long-term commitment of the force to provide for equitable participation of both official language groups.
I am not at liberty at this time to go into the details of the proposals of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher). However, I am sure the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) will be hearing from the Solicitor General concerning these matters in the not too distant future.
